ATLAS labs booklet.text:
ATLAS Institute Research Labs at the University of Colorado Boulder focus on interdisciplinary research combining technology, design, and human interaction.

The poster features eight labs:

- ACME Lab: Creative technology and computational media.
- Emergent Nanomaterials Lab: Nanomaterials and advanced fabrication.
- Programmable Reality Lab: Interactive physical systems and programmable environments.
- Unstable Design Lab: Experimental and interactive design.
- Brain Music Lab: Neuroscience, music, and human experience.
- Living Matter Lab: Bio-inspired materials and design.
- TYPO Lab: Creative computing and emerging technologies.
- Utility Research Lab: Human-centered technology and interactive systems.

Overall Focus: HCI, creative technology, physical computing, material innovation, and interdisciplinary design research.

Programmable Reality Lab.text: Full name: Programmable Reality Lab. Short name: PRL. People may call it "the lab", "this lab", "PRL" or "Programmable Reality Lab"; all mean this lab. The Programmable Reality Lab (PRL) belongs to the ATLAS Institute at the University of Colorado Boulder. It is led by Prof. Ryo Suzuki. Its students are Hye-Young Jo, Keiichi Ihara, Ada Yi Zhao, Sean Xiaoan Liu and Ziru Wei (five students).

PRL research theme.text:
Today we program computers we live with.
Tomorrow we program the whole environment we live in.

The goal of Programmable Reality Lab is to make our whole living environment dynamic, interactive, and programmable. With that, we envision to transform our living space into a dynamic medium―instead of constraining ourselves into a flat rectangle screen, we envision to make our entire world a dynamic and expressive canvas, as if we are living in a computer, rather than we are living with computers. Towards this seamlessly coupled digital and physical world, we pursue both visually and physically programmable reality by exploring novel interactive technologies enabled by AR/VR, robotics, and shape-changing interfaces.

PRL philosophy.text:
Philosophy of the Programmable Reality Lab (PRL), by its director Prof. Ryo Suzuki:

First and foremost, student success and happiness are the first priorities. Everything else is secondary.

Do What You Are Most Excited About:
In research, many factors contribute to success and happiness, such as the number of publications, recognition, awards, and so on. However, I strongly believe that the most important factor is that you are excited and passionate about what you are doing.
Therefore, the principle is simple: follow your heart. Do what excites you, and don’t do what doesn’t. Life is short. You are not doing research for me. You should be doing it for yourself.
Sometimes students already have a clear vision and goal. If that’s the case, that’s great and go for it. If not, my first priority, especially in the first year, is to help you figure out what you are truly excited and passionate about.
This is actually a harder process than publishing a paper. But I want you to pursue this during your PhD. Your goal might be too big for five years? That’s fine. You might change along the way? That’s fine too. What matters is having a clear direction rather than chasing random projects. Try to think about how you want to be remembered and how you want to be recognized.
Your inner passion is by default invisible from the outside. For instance, I cannot ultimately know what truly excites you the most. Therefore, it comes from dialogue with yourself. Every person is shaped by accumulated personal experiences, which in turn shape values, ways of thinking, and perspectives on the world. These experiences should guide your research interests. So, please try to think about why you are doing what you are doing, and why you not someone else.
During your first years, I may ask you these questions often—not to pressure you, but to help you identify and pursue what excites you. Sometimes this means revisiting past research and reflecting on what aspects sparked your excitement. Sometimes it means connecting dots into a bigger vision. In any case, remember: Do your PhD research for yourself, not for me. Following your excitement is the most important foundation for success and happiness in your life among many other things.
Outside of research, we also strive to ensure that you are happy and satisfied with your PhD life. I will do my best to accommodate your needs whenever possible. Once again, our first priority is always student success and happiness, and we act based on this first principle.
